title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment to test whether integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications from an LLM compared with an LLM‑only pipeline. Using a NetConfArena‑style emulator and a closed, deterministic task corpus (N=240 paired intents; in‑distribution 60%, distribution‑shift 20%, adversarial‑prompt 20%), each task produced a single shared initial LLM candidate (shared_initial_candidate semantics); the guarded condition could invoke up to one validator‑triggered repair. The primary estimand was the paired difference in unsafe‑apply rate (GVR minus LLM‑only). All 240 paired tasks were scored safe under both arms (baseline and guarded), yielding an observed paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; exact McNemar p = 1.0). Deterministic reconciliation of execution artifacts shows the null result occurred because the single shared initial generation was already validator‑acceptable for every task, so no repair was invoked. We interpret this outcome as an evidence‑grounded operational lesson: under shared_initial_candidate evaluation semantics, a verifier can only alter outcomes when the shared initial generation violates verifier checks or when repairs are triggered; therefore measuring a verifier’s benefit requires task generators, adversaries, or sampling semantics that produce verifier‑failing initial candidates. We report the preregistered design, execution manifest, statistical analysis, and limitations, and we discuss implications for future emulation‑grounded NetOps evaluations.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into device configurations and to assist NetOps workflows. Prior work emphasizes executable, emulation‑grounded evaluation to reveal operational failure modes beyond syntactic errors [1]. A recurring architectural response is a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pattern: LLM generation followed by deterministic validation and iterative repair [2,3]. We preregistered a paired experiment to answer a focused, confirmatory question: does adding a deterministic verifier (GVR) reduce unsafe configuration applications relative to LLM‑only outputs in an emulation‑grounded benchmark? Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired study executed on a NetConfArena‑style emulator (study id: study‑cand‑1‑gvr‑verifier‑adversarial‑2026‑08‑01); (2) complete, archived execution and analysis artifacts; and (3) a failure‑analytic interpretation of a null (zero‑difference) outcome with practical recommendations for future evaluations.
sections.related_work: Executable, emulation‑grounded NetOps benchmarks have been proposed to evaluate closed‑loop LLM agents in risk‑free networks and to surface planning and execution failures not captured by static text metrics [1]. Syntax‑ and semantics‑oriented automated configuration repair methods have shown strong repair rates in constrained settings [2], while position and survey papers argue that operational reliability for agentic NetOps depends more on surrounding machinery (verification, gating, tool orchestration) than on models alone [3,4]. Uncertainty estimation and calibration techniques are recognized as important gating signals for operator reliance, but domain‑specific calibration evidence for NetOps is limited [5]. Our study builds on these strands by deploying a paired, preregistered GVR vs LLM‑only comparison in an emulation‑grounded testbed.
sections.methodology: Design: We preregistered a paired binary design comparing (A) baseline LLM‑only and (B) guarded GVR (deterministic verifier plus up to one repair) using shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial generation per task reused across both arms). Primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline (absolute paired difference in unsafe‑apply rate). Sampling: N=240 paired tasks blocked into topology/vendor clusters; in‑distribution 60% (144), distribution‑shift 20% (48), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48). Model and pipeline: single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) produced the shared initial candidate; the guarded adapter invoked deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and was allowed one repair attempt if the validator failed. The emulator executed final configurations and deterministically scored unsafe_apply vs safe_apply. Analysis: primary paired difference estimated with paired bootstrap percentile CIs and an exact McNemar two‑sided test; preregistered sensitivity analyses addressed verifier/simulator inconsistencies and infrastructure failures. All design elements, inclusion/exclusion rules, and analysis executors were frozen prior to data collection.
sections.results: Execution: The run completed per the preregistered manifest: 240 paired tasks, 480 episodes, and 240 shared initial model calls. Primary outcome: every paired episode was scored safe under both arms (baseline and guarded). The observed paired difference = 0.00 with 95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Contingency counts: n11=240, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Deterministic reconciliation confirms a single shared initial candidate was submitted per task and that the validator accepted that candidate in every episode; accordingly no repair action occurred for any guarded episode. Secondary metrics (repair counts, model call budgets, latency buckets) are reported in the archived artifacts; repair_attempts = 0 for all guarded episodes, and total model calls used = 240 (one shared initial call per task).
sections.discussion: Interpretation: The confirmatory hypothesis (that GVR reduces unsafe applications) was not supported; the observed null result is itself scientifically informative under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics. In this execution the verifier could not affect outcomes because initial candidates passed validation universally. This shows that (a) when the LLM produces valid configurations, a downstream deterministic verifier will not change the applied configuration, and (b) demonstrating verifier benefits experimentally requires task generators, sampling semantics, or adversaries that produce verifier‑failing initial outputs. Practical implications: future evaluations should (i) include independent initial draws per arm or allow more repair budget, (ii) expand adversary strength and adversarial‑testing procedures, and (iii) vary verifier coverage (symbolic vs semantic checks) to probe where GVR delivers operational benefits. Limitations: emulation scope (synthetic device images and parameterized tasks) limits external validity to production, single‑model scope (one hosted model) limits generality across models or prompts, the shared_initial_candidate design intentionally constrained per preregistration (see Methods) and therefore precluded generator variability between arms, and the adversary generation procedure was bounded by the preregistered attacker protocol. These limitations are detailed in the archived manifest.
sections.conclusion: We conducted a fully preregistered, paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a generate–validate–repair pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcomes were safe in every paired episode under both the LLM‑only and GVR arms, producing a zero paired difference. The null result is evidence‑grounded and highlights an important experimental design point: under shared_initial_candidate semantics only validator‑failing initial candidates can allow the verifier to change outcomes. We provide the preregistration, execution manifest, analysis artifacts, and a diagnostic interpretation to guide future NetOps evaluations that aim to quantify verifier‑orchestration benefits under realistic distribution shift and adversarial conditions.

disclosure_statement: Models and prompt: The study used a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) called by the registered adapter 'hosted_netops_gvr_v1'. The exact immutable initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Human role and autonomy: a human Research Director selected the broad topic family (Generative AI / LLMs for NetOps) and constrained the initial master prompt pre‑lock. After the autonomy lock the research run (literature selection, preregistration, experiment design, execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, and revision) was performed autonomously by the archived pipeline; no manual human editing of technical manuscript content occurred post‑lock. Preregistration and artifacts: the experiment was preregistered (study id study‑cand‑1‑gvr‑verifier‑adversarial‑2026‑08‑01) and executed per the frozen plan; artifacts, raw outputs, execution manifest, analysis executors, and compiled paper sources are archived alongside the run. Frameworks and verifier: the guarded pipeline used the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as the verifier and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Execution semantics: the run adopted shared_initial_candidate semantics as specified in the preregistration (one initial generation per task reused across paired arms); only validator‑triggered repair could create paired divergences. Deviations: no post‑preregistration changes to the scientific design occurred. Pre‑lock development: prior infrastructure development and rehearsals occurred but were explicitly excluded from the final empirical evidence; only artifacts produced under the post‑lock workflow are reported as results.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidates failing validation.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed attacker protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.
Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 provides a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier.
